# Wirecard / Jan Marsalek Public-Fraud Trail: Evidence-Based Reconstruction

## Executive assessment

The supplied evidence supports a clear public-fraud trail concerning Wirecard’s financial reporting, the credibility of its cash balances and third-party-acquiring revenues, and failures across several oversight mechanisms. It does **not**, however, provide sufficient evidence to reconstruct Jan Marsalek’s disappearance, establish when he disappeared, identify his location, or attribute specific conduct to him. Those matters must therefore be treated as unresolved and outside the evidentiary scope of this report.

The strongest conclusion supported by the record is that Wirecard’s public communications in April 2020 presented the KPMG investigation as having found no incriminating evidence of balance-sheet forgery, while the underlying investigation reportedly could not verify key revenues and approximately €1 billion in trust-account balances. Two months later, Wirecard acknowledged that €1.9 billion in reported bank balances probably did not exist and filed for insolvency. The sequence indicates a major contradiction between Wirecard’s April public framing and the subsequent collapse of the company’s reported financial position. ([S1](https://www.wirecard.com/2020/04/22/wirecard-ag-kpmg-special-review-lasts-until-april-27-2020-analysis-so-far-provides-no-evidence-of-balance-sheet-manipulation); [S2](https://safe-frankfurt.de/fileadmin/user_upload/editor_common/Policy_Center/SAFE_Policy_White_Paper_74.pdf))

The evidence also supports the assessment that Wirecard’s collapse was not attributable to a single failed control. The European Parliament policy study describes failures involving internal controls, the supervisory board, external auditing, audit and financial-reporting oversight, and BaFin, Germany’s financial supervisor. ([S2](https://safe-frankfurt.de/fileadmin/user_upload/editor_common/Policy_Center/SAFE_Policy_White_Paper_74.pdf))

## Scope and source methodology

Only two source records were supplied:

| Source ID | Source | Evidentiary character |
|---|---|---|
| **S1** | Wirecard regulatory announcement distributed through DGAP/EQS | Primary company statement dated 28 April 2020, concerning the KPMG special investigation |
| **S2** | Langenbucher, Leuz, Kra(h)nen, and Pelizzon policy study for the European Parliament | Secondary analytical study completed in 2020, incorporating a timeline and references to other materials |

The report distinguishes among:

- **Documented facts:** statements directly contained in the supplied sources.
- **Allegations:** accusations or reported suspicions described by the study.
- **Assessments:** conclusions drawn by the study’s authors or by this report.
- **Uncertainty:** matters that the sources do not establish.

The evidence contains a small metadata inconsistency: S1’s URL refers to 22 April 2020, while the supplied document content is a 28 April 2020 announcement reporting delivery of the KPMG report. The report uses the date stated in the announcement itself. ([S1](https://www.wirecard.com/2020/04/22/wirecard-ag-kpmg-special-review-lasts-until-april-27-2020-analysis-so-far-provides-no-evidence-of-balance-sheet-manipulation))

## Chronology of the public-fraud trail

### Early warnings and critical information

The policy study records allegations concerning Wirecard’s accounting practices as early as 2008. A shareholder association reportedly alleged that Wirecard’s margins were implausibly high and that customer deposits had been treated as Wirecard’s own cash. The study also records the 2016 Zatarra report, which accused Wirecard of corruption, fraud, and money laundering. These are allegations reported by S2, not findings independently established in the supplied primary evidence. ([S2](https://safe-frankfurt.de/fileadmin/user_upload/editor_common/Policy_Center/SAFE_Policy_White_Paper_74.pdf))

From 2015 onward, the Financial Times published reports questioning Wirecard’s accounting and corporate structure. According to S2, employees in Singapore later provided internal documents to Financial Times journalists because they were concerned that an internal investigation had been suppressed. The identity and full evidentiary position of those whistleblowers are not established in the supplied sources. ([S2](https://safe-frankfurt.de/fileadmin/user_upload/editor_common/Policy_Center/SAFE_Policy_White_Paper_74.pdf))

S2 presents these warnings as potentially important information channels that were not adequately acted upon. Its authors emphasize, however, that hindsight bias must be avoided because warnings can be accurate, mistaken, malicious, or motivated by market manipulation. ([S2](https://safe-frankfurt.de/fileadmin/user_upload/editor_common/Policy_Center/SAFE_Policy_White_Paper_74.pdf))

### 2019: regulatory intervention and short-sale restrictions

On 30 January 2019, the Financial Times reportedly published an article concerning a Singapore investigation and alleged forged or backdated contracts used to increase revenues. On 15 February 2019, BaFin directed FREP, Germany’s Financial Reporting Enforcement Panel, to examine Wirecard’s interim accounts as of 30 June 2018. ([S2](https://safe-frankfurt.de/fileadmin/user_upload/editor_common/Policy_Center/SAFE_Policy_White_Paper_74.pdf))

On 18 February 2019, BaFin prohibited the establishment or increase of net short positions in Wirecard shares until 18 April 2019. ESMA approved the measure. According to S2, the intervention was justified by a combination of falling prices, increased volatility, and concerns about market confidence. The study’s authors assess the measure critically, arguing that a short-sale ban could prevent negative information from being reflected in market prices and might lead investors to infer that the regulator possessed information favorable to Wirecard. ([S2](https://safe-frankfurt.de/fileadmin/user_upload/editor_common/Policy_Center/SAFE_Policy_White_Paper_74.pdf))

BaFin also filed criminal complaints against Financial Times journalists and short sellers on suspicion of market manipulation, according to the timeline in S2. This is evidence of regulatory action, not proof that the journalists or short sellers committed market manipulation. ([S2](https://safe-frankfurt.de/fileadmin/user_upload/editor_common/Policy_Center/SAFE_Policy_White_Paper_74.pdf))

In October 2019, Wirecard hired KPMG to conduct an independent forensic investigation into accusations published in the media and online. ([S2](https://safe-frankfurt.de/fileadmin/user_upload/editor_common/Policy_Center/SAFE_Policy_White_Paper_74.pdf))

## The KPMG investigation and the April 2020 company statements

### Wirecard’s public position

On 28 April 2020, Wirecard announced that it had received KPMG’s special audit report. The announcement stated that no incriminating evidence for the public allegations of balance-sheet forgery had been identified. It further stated that, across the four investigation areas—third-party acquiring, merchant cash advance/digital lending, India, and Singapore—KPMG had identified no significant findings requiring adjustment of the 2016–2018 annual accounts. ([S1](https://www.wirecard.com/2020/04/22/wirecard-ag-kpmg-special-review-lasts-until-april-27-2020-analysis-so-far-provides-no-evidence-of-balance-sheet-manipulation))

Wirecard also stated that the documents and audit procedures available during the ordinary audits had been sufficient to prove third-party-acquiring revenues. It acknowledged, however, that KPMG’s heightened forensic requirements could not be fully satisfied because relevant data were primarily controlled by third parties. Wirecard claimed that more than 200 million data sets relating to December 2019 had been supplied to KPMG and that no deviations had been identified between reported revenues and account balances in that testing. ([S1](https://www.wirecard.com/2020/04/22/wirecard-ag-kpmg-special-review-lasts-until-april-27-2020-analysis-so-far-provides-no-evidence-of-balance-sheet-manipulation))

The announcement also admitted documentation and organizational weaknesses, while presenting Wirecard’s Global Compliance Organization and external consultants as remedial measures begun in 2019. The release of the annual accounts and annual press conference was postponed. ([S1](https://www.wirecard.com/2020/04/22/wirecard-ag-kpmg-special-review-lasts-until-april-27-2020-analysis-so-far-provides-no-evidence-of-balance-sheet-manipulation))

### What the policy study says KPMG actually established

S2 describes the KPMG report differently from Wirecard’s public summary. According to the study, KPMG could not verify approximately €1 billion in trust accounts, representing roughly one-quarter of Wirecard’s balance sheet at the time. The study says KPMG attributed this inability to insufficient documentation by Wirecard and its third-party acquirers. ([S2](https://safe-frankfurt.de/fileadmin/user_upload/editor_common/Policy_Center/SAFE_Policy_White_Paper_74.pdf))

S2 further states that KPMG could neither confirm nor refute whether revenues from particular third-party-acquiring relationships existed or were correct in amount. The study quotes the KPMG conclusion that the investigation could not make a positive statement that the revenues existed and were accurate, nor a positive statement that they were fictitious or misstated. ([S2](https://safe-frankfurt.de/fileadmin/user_upload/editor_common/Policy_Center/SAFE_Policy_White_Paper_74.pdf))

This distinction is critical. “No incriminating evidence identified” is not equivalent to “the alleged revenues and cash balances were independently verified.” The available evidence indicates that KPMG’s inability to obtain or verify essential records limited the conclusions that could be drawn. That is an evidentiary limitation, not an exoneration.

## Missing cash and the collapse of Wirecard’s position

The public-fraud trail escalated sharply in June 2020. On 22 June, Wirecard’s board reportedly stated that bank balances of €1.9 billion held in trust accounts probably did not exist and that the third-party business might be incorrect in the manner previously described. On 25 June, Wirecard filed for insolvency because of impending insolvency and over-indebtedness. ([S2](https://safe-frankfurt.de/fileadmin/user_upload/editor_common/Policy_Center/SAFE_Policy_White_Paper_74.pdf))

S2 also reports that EY refused to sign off Wirecard’s 2019 accounts after determining that bank confirmations concerning escrow-account balances were forged. EY reportedly described the matter as involving clear indications of a sophisticated fraud designed to deceive multiple parties across jurisdictions. These statements are presented in S2 as reported developments and should not be treated as a final judicial finding of criminal responsibility. ([S2](https://safe-frankfurt.de/fileadmin/user_upload/editor_common/Policy_Center/SAFE_Policy_White_Paper_74.pdf))

The numerical progression is therefore central:

| Date | Publicly documented development | Significance |
|---|---|---|
| 28 April 2020 | Wirecard says KPMG found no incriminating evidence requiring account adjustments | Company presents investigation as broadly non-exculpatory |
| 28 April 2020 | KPMG reportedly unable to verify approximately €1 billion in trust accounts and certain TPA revenues | Critical evidence remained unresolved |
| 22 June 2020 | Wirecard says €1.9 billion in trust-account balances probably did not exist | Reported cash position collapses |
| 25 June 2020 | Wirecard files for insolvency | Financial crisis becomes formal insolvency |

([S1](https://www.wirecard.com/2020/04/22/wirecard-ag-kpmg-special-review-lasts-until-april-27-2020-analysis-so-far-provides-no-evidence-of-balance-sheet-manipulation); [S2](https://safe-frankfurt.de/fileadmin/user_upload/editor_common/Policy_Center/SAFE_Policy_White_Paper_74.pdf))

## Supervisory and audit failures

S2 characterizes Wirecard as a failure of five lines of defense:

1. Wirecard’s internal control system.
2. The supervisory board.
3. The external audit.
4. Bodies overseeing financial reporting and auditing.
5. BaFin as market supervisor.

([S2](https://safe-frankfurt.de/fileadmin/user_upload/editor_common/Policy_Center/SAFE_Policy_White_Paper_74.pdf))

The study identifies several structural problems:

- Germany’s two-step financial-reporting enforcement system gave FREP an initial role before BaFin could fully exercise its authority.
- FREP relied substantially on the company’s voluntary cooperation and lacked statutory investigative powers.
- BaFin’s responsibilities and powers were fragmented between market supervision, financial-reporting enforcement, and banking supervision.
- Wirecard’s parent company was not treated as a bank or financial holding company, limiting the banking-supervision tools available against the parent.
- Audit oversight lacked transparency because inspection results for individual audit firms were not publicly disclosed.
- External audit incentives were weakened by audit-market concentration, limited auditor liability, and the difficulty outsiders face in evaluating audit quality.
- Supervisory responses to whistleblowers, critical journalism, and short sellers were judged insufficient by the study’s authors.

([S2](https://safe-frankfurt.de/fileadmin/user_upload/editor_common/Policy_Center/SAFE_Policy_White_Paper_74.pdf))

The study’s recommendations included making BaFin the sole competent authority for financial-reporting enforcement, strengthening investigative powers, requiring effective internal controls, strengthening audit committees, increasing auditor accountability, protecting whistleblowers, restricting short-sale bans to more clearly systemic situations, and considering a European Single Capital Market Supervisor. These are policy recommendations, not evidence that the proposed reforms have been implemented or that they would necessarily have prevented the fraud. ([S2](https://safe-frankfurt.de/fileadmin/user_upload/editor_common/Policy_Center/SAFE_Policy_White_Paper_74.pdf))

## Jan Marsalek’s disappearance: evidentiary limits

The supplied materials do not contain a substantiated account of Jan Marsalek’s disappearance. They do not establish:

- the date or circumstances of his disappearance;
- whether he left Germany voluntarily or under coercion;
- his destination or current whereabouts;
- whether he possessed, moved, or concealed Wirecard assets;
- whether he participated in the alleged accounting conduct;
- whether he acted with other individuals;
- whether his disappearance was connected to the missing €1.9 billion.

Accordingly, no responsible evidence-based report can connect Marsalek personally to the public-fraud trail on the basis of the supplied sources. The materials discuss Wirecard executives, management, auditors, regulators, whistleblowers, journalists, short sellers, and third-party acquirers in general terms, but they do not provide a source-supported Marsalek-specific evidentiary chain. ([S2](https://safe-frankfurt.de/fileadmin/user_upload/editor_common/Policy_Center/SAFE_Policy_White_Paper_74.pdf))

The appropriate conclusion is therefore narrow but definite: **the supplied evidence documents a Wirecard financial-reporting and oversight crisis, but it does not establish the role of Jan Marsalek in that crisis or explain his disappearance.** Any stronger statement would require additional authoritative sources, such as court records, official investigative findings, insolvency materials, parliamentary evidence, or verified law-enforcement notices.

## Overall conclusion

The public record supplied here shows a progression from long-standing allegations and whistleblower information, through regulatory and media conflict, to a company-commissioned forensic investigation that left major issues unresolved, followed by the acknowledgement that €1.9 billion in reported trust-account balances probably did not exist and the company’s insolvency.

My assessment is that Wirecard’s 28 April statement should be read as a carefully limited corporate communication rather than a definitive clearance. Its wording emphasized the absence of “incriminating evidence” and the absence of findings requiring accounting adjustments, but the evidence summarized by S2 indicates that KPMG could not verify essential revenues and cash balances. The subsequent disappearance of €1.9 billion from the reported financial position makes the April statement materially misleading in effect, even though the supplied evidence does not by itself establish the legal elements of a deliberately false disclosure.

The strongest supported explanation for the delayed detection is institutional fragmentation combined with overreliance on company-provided documentation, weak escalation of external warnings, audit limitations, and insufficiently forceful public enforcement. The Marsalek component remains unresolved in this evidentiary record and should not be inferred from the broader Wirecard findings.

## References

Langenbucher, K., Leuz, C., Kra(h)nen, J. P., & Pelizzon, L. (2020). *What are the wider supervisory implications of the Wirecard case?* Economic Governance Support Unit, European Parliament. [https://safe-frankfurt.de/fileadmin/user_upload/editor_common/Policy_Center/SAFE_Policy_White_Paper_74.pdf](https://safe-frankfurt.de/fileadmin/user_upload/editor_common/Policy_Center/SAFE_Policy_White_Paper_74.pdf)

Wirecard AG. (2020, April 28). *Wirecard AG: KPMG delivers report on special investigation*. DGAP/EQS regulatory announcement. [https://www.wirecard.com/2020/04/22/wirecard-ag-kpmg-special-review-lasts-until-april-27-2020-analysis-so-far-provides-no-evidence-of-balance-sheet-manipulation](https://www.wirecard.com/2020/04/22/wirecard-ag-kpmg-special-review-lasts-until-april-27-2020-analysis-so-far-provides-no-evidence-of-balance-sheet-manipulation)
